rv.q: For pure Biblical hyperbole, Stephen Schwartz’s musical version of the 1998. DreamWorks animated film will take some beating.
The music is miraculous; if only there was storytelling to match.
For all its energy and endeavour, though, this is a piece of theatre that gets lost in the desert.
But the show is too inconsistent in quality and vision to do itself justice.
Old Testament grit is rather absent.
Scott Schwartz’s production is stuffed full of imagination but it is so excessive and outsized that it overwhelms the emotional drama, sucking away any intimacy between the actors.
As a stage version of an animated classic, The Prince of Egypt delivers in spades.
This staging is driven by a pace and an energy that carries the audience with it.

Firstly, the ensemble cast of this show must be praised. One minute they form a temple, the next the River Nile running red with blood, and in between they are the Burning Bush. Sparsely dressed in Ann Hould-Ward's lacklustre costumes, the intense, physical energy this company brings is impressive. ...
The staging often looks gorgeous, with a series of sandstone platforms enhanced by massive projections that wrap around the stage and auditorium.
It just about held my attention throughout, but the songs are, ‘When You Believe’ excepted, largely unmemorable.
But the collective efforts of a thoroughly committed team make this an enjoyable enough outing for those who like their theatre big, sincere and occasionally spectacular.
Constantly going from zero to emotional overload, it’s so effortful it’s enervating.
But the sheer size of the Dominion is a disadvantage.

The Prince of Egypt, based on the 1998 inaugural feature from Dreamworks Animation, is a biblical pageant that comes with all the weighty, earnest and portentous air of an end-of-year Nativity project, though on a considerably larger budget.

The Prince of Egypt is an absolute extravaganza – lavish costumes, acrobatic physical theatre, innovative staging, stunning vocals and a gut-wrenching storyline, all rousingly contained within the score of Stephen Schwartz.
The Prince of Egypt is certainly epic, and needs to be seen to be believed.
While newcomers will know no different, I fear fans of the film will be left wanting to return to the animation.

The Dominion has an almost unrivalled track record in providing a home for truly awful musicals and this turgid offering from Stephen Schwartz based on the 1998. Dreamworks animated movie of the same name is a notable addition to the list.
This musical about Moses is not one of them.

cn.t: Schwartz's Biblical epic delivers spectacular staging and powerful vocals, but critics find it strained and lacking in nuance. The hardworking ensemble impresses, yet the show feels caught between animated spectacle and theatrical depth.
